chapters.title: Chapter 2: Quantitative Frameworks for Geopolitical Risk

lessons.title: Building a Geopolitical Risk Index for Indian Markets

body.text: A geopolitical risk index is not a crystal ball. It is a disciplined way to convert scattered channel-level signals into one comparable number, so the same yardstick applies whether today's stress is coming from oil, the rupee, or capital flight.

children.text: Chapter 1 built a qualitative scorecard: for a given headline, did the trade, commodity, currency, and capital flow channels fire or not. That scorecard works well after the fact, once a full episode like Balakot, Covid-19, or the Russia-Ukraine war has played out and you can look back at the data. It is less useful on a live Tuesday morning when three of the four channels look mildly stressed and you need one number to anchor a conversation with a portfolio committee. This lesson turns Chapter 1's scorecard into an actual index: a set of India-specific market indicators, standardised onto a common scale, combined into a single composite reading you can compute and track daily.
Two Ways to Build a Geopolitical Risk Index: News-Based vs Market-Based

columns.label: News-Based (e.g. the Caldara-Iacoviello GPR Index)
points: Counts the share of newspaper articles mentioning war, terrorism, or geopolitical tension each month
Captures sentiment and attention, useful for comparing risk across many decades of history
Not India-specific, and reacts to what gets written about, not necessarily what is actually priced
Typically updated monthly, too slow for a live portfolio decision

columns.label: Market-Based (This Lesson's Approach)
points: Built from actual India-specific price and flow data: freight rates, crude oil, USD/INR, FPI flows
Updates daily, fast enough to inform a live decision
Directly measures transmission through the four channels, not just media attention
Requires choosing indicators and weights carefully, a modelling judgment with real trade-offs

children.text: Choosing the Inputs: One Indicator Per Channel

Keep the first version of this index simple: one primary indicator per channel, each defined so that a higher reading always means more stress. That sign convention matters. A freight cost spike, a crude oil spike, a currency volatility spike, and an FPI outflow spike should all point the same direction, so the four numbers can be combined without flipping signs and introducing avoidable errors.

body.caption: One indicator per channel, chosen so higher always means more stress

cells: Container freight rate index (India-Europe route), % change vs its 90-day average
Reacts within days to a blocked route or a disrupted supply chain, well ahead of official trade data releases
Brent crude, % change vs its 90-day average
The single commodity with the widest, fastest economy-wide transmission into India
USD/INR 30-day realised volatility vs its 1-year average
Volatility, not just the level, tells you the market is actively repricing currency risk right now
FPI net equity outflow, 5-day cumulative, vs its 90-day average
Captures the fastest-moving of the four channels directly, without waiting for month-end data

markDefs.definition: A statistic showing how many standard deviations a reading is from its own historical mean. A z-score of 0 is exactly average; a z-score of 2 means the reading is two standard deviations above its typical range, unusual but not extreme.

, using a rolling mean and standard deviation computed over a lookback window, typically 90 days for price and flow indicators and a full year for a volatility measure like currency vol, so the window itself captures a reasonable range of normal market conditions.

body.caption: z_i is the standardised reading for channel i; X_i is today's raw reading; mu_i and sigma_i are that indicator's rolling mean and standard deviation over the lookback window.

children.text: Weighting and Aggregating Into a Composite Score

With four z-scores in hand, the next decision is how to weight them. An institutional desk with enough historical episodes might estimate weights through regression against realised market drawdowns. For a first version of this index, equal weighting is the more defensible starting choice: it is transparent, it does not pretend to a precision the data does not support, and it is easy for a portfolio committee to audit. Refining the weights is exactly the kind of extension worth revisiting once you have backtested the simple version against more episodes than this course can cover.

body.caption: With equal weights (w_i = 1/n for every channel), this collapses to a simple average of the four channel z-scores, the version used through the rest of this lesson.
Risk bands for the composite GRI reading

cells: Business as usual; no channel showing meaningful stress
One or two channels mildly elevated; worth watching, not yet acting on
Multiple channels stressed at once; a reading in the range this lesson associates with the Russia-Ukraine war
Every channel stressed simultaneously; a reading in the range this lesson associates with the Covid-19 crash

children.text: Backtesting the Index Against Chapter 1's Three Episodes

body.title: Illustrative Composite GRI Reading at Each Episode's Peak Stress

body.text: Run this methodology back over Chapter 1's three episodes and it recovers the same pattern that lesson built by hand: Balakot stays in the Low band, since none of the four channels ever moved far from normal. The Russia-Ukraine war lands in the Elevated band, three channels clearly stressed. Covid-19 pushes into the Severe band, every channel breaking at once. A quantitative index is only useful if it agrees with a careful qualitative read of history; this is that check.

Treat this index as contemporaneous, not predictive. It tells you how stressed the four channels are right now, not what happens next; a Severe reading can persist, worsen, or fade within days. It is also sensitive to the choices behind it: which indicators you pick, how long a lookback window you use, and how you weight the channels can all shift a reading between bands. And it only sees what it is built to see; a channel this course has not modelled, such as a cyberattack on financial infrastructure or a sudden technology export ban, would not show up until it also moved one of these four indicators.

body.title: Compute a Channel Z-Score
body.prompt: A new reading comes in for the currency channel: USD/INR 30-day realised volatility is 8.6%, against a 1-year average of 5.5% and a standard deviation of 1.5%. What is this channel's z-score?
body.explanation: z = (8.6 - 5.5) / 1.5 = 2.07. On its own, that already sits close to the Elevated/Severe boundary for a single channel, before it is even combined with the other three into the composite reading.

body.title: Read Behind the Composite Number
body.scenario: You check today's four channel z-scores: trade 1.9, commodity 0.4, currency 0.6, capital flows 2.3. The equal-weighted composite GRI comes out to 1.3, placing it in the Elevated band.
body.prompt: Two channels are clearly stressed and two are calm. Is reading the composite number alone the right way to size this up, or does it hide something a fund manager should know? What would you check next?
body.modelAnswer: The composite number alone hides useful information here. An Elevated reading of 1.3 could come from four mildly stressed channels or, as in this case, from two sharply stressed channels and two calm ones averaging out to the same headline number. That distinction matters: a shock concentrated in trade and capital flows, without a matching commodity or currency move, likely points to something narrower, such as a shipping disruption or a sanctions-driven capital flight event, rather than a broad-based energy shock. A fund manager should always look at the per-channel breakdown the underlying function already returns, not just the composite, check which specific live headline is driving the trade and capital-flow readings, and watch whether the commodity and currency channels start moving too, which would be the signal this is broadening rather than staying contained.

body.title: Set Up Your Own GRI Tracker
steps: Choose your own indicator per channel if you prefer a different proxy than this lesson's, for example a Baltic Dry Index reading instead of a container freight index for the trade channel
Decide your lookback window for the rolling mean and standard deviation; this lesson uses 90 days for price and flow indicators and one year for currency volatility
Adapt the Python function from this lesson to compute your four z-scores and composite GRI from a small spreadsheet of daily readings
Backtest your index against at least the three Chapter 1 episodes, Balakot, Covid-19, and the Russia-Ukraine war, and check whether it classifies each one into the band you would expect
Keep this tracker running; the next lesson uses it directly to build scenario analysis and stress tests for a portfolio

body.text: The index methodology, indicator choices, weights, and worked-example figures in this lesson are illustrative and built for teaching purposes. This is not a live index maintained or published by this platform, and the historical episode readings shown in the backtest are approximate reconstructions, not officially reported data. This is educational content, not investment advice.

points: A geopolitical risk index converts Chapter 1's qualitative four-channel scorecard into one comparable number, built from India-specific market and flow data rather than news-mining alone

Standardising each channel's raw indicator into a z-score, using a rolling mean and standard deviation, is what makes differently-scaled indicators, percentage moves, volatility, and rupee-crore flows, combinable
An equal-weighted average of the four channel z-scores is a transparent starting methodology; risk bands, Low, Moderate, Elevated, Severe, translate the composite score into a usable read
Backtested against Chapter 1's episodes, this methodology classifies Balakot as Low, the Russia-Ukraine war as Elevated, and Covid-19 as Severe, matching the qualitative pattern built earlier by hand

The composite number is a summary, not the full picture; always check the per-channel breakdown behind it, and remember this index is contemporaneous, not predictive, before the next lesson builds scenario analysis and stress tests on top of it
